doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: Glen Gray, Casa Loma, and Dean Hudson's band in Atlanta
summary: Glen Gray's real name, and a chance meeting in Atlanta with Dean Hudson and Casa Loma trombonist Billy Rauch.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Yes. Glen Gray. His right name is Glen Gray Knoblauch. K-N-O-B-L-A-U-C-H. Glen Gray Knoblauch.
Well he knew that that part probably wasn’t best for his professional career.
It’s easier to say Glen Gray. He had some later to be famous people in and out of that band.

I met one of them in Atlanta. During my AMA career I went to Atlanta to some kind of a scientific or political meeting, medical, and got to the hotel, The Marriot I think it was, early in the evening, and I heard music downstairs somewhere below the lobby. And there was nothing to do until the next morning so I went down there, and it was the dying moments of a cocktail party. And the man who the party was for was the man who was Secretary of State from Georgia, I’ve forgotten his name now, a well known Secretary of State. But the cocktail was for him. But it had pretty much broken up. There were only half a dozen people sitting around, the band was still playing a little bit. And I stood there and watched and listened a bit, close to the band. And pretty soon the leader came around and said “you like this music, don’t you.” I said “yes I do.” And he said “did you hear us play the Casa Loma theme song?” I said “you mean ‘Smoke Rings?’” He said “do you know that the trombone player who played that in the theme song is sitting in the brass section here?” I says “you mean Billy Rush?” He says “yes.” I says “well I know who he is,” and I met him. And this man’s name was Dean Hudson, was the orchestra leader, and he played society and college bands around Georgia and Florida and Texas, and a lot of famous bands know about him and played with him and he became a great friend and we used to correspond, and he sent me records that he’d made. And he’s probably since died because very few of my contemporaries survive. But he was a very fine man.
